analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We will continue with arguments in 74-215. Mr. Tuttle, you may proceed when you're ready. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, yesterday I argued that a corporate officer with a responsible relation to a condition of adulteration may be charged with a violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. I also argued that a chief executive officer, or a president of a corporation, generally has the power and the responsibility to place him in a responsible relation to a condition of violation. This, I think, is accurate as far as it goes, but it only states half of the equation. The other half of the equation is the matter of affirmative defenses. The evidence we have been discussing is evidence which the government submits is sufficient to establish a prima facie case. Beyond that, there is the question of defenses which an otherwise responsible corporate executive might be able to raise. I want to discuss this morning the question of defenses, but I can only do so in the context of the statutory scheme that Congress has created. A discussion of the duties or defenses under the Act would be meaningless without an understanding of the special nature of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The 1938 Act deals with the distribution of all foods, drugs, cosmetics, and medical devices. Matters which vitally affect the health of every citizen. No person need enter the food business, or the cosmetic business, or the business of distributing medical devices. But on those who do, Congress has imposed the very highest duty of care. Dottowike teaches, for instance, that Congress imposed upon those who deal in these vital commodities the risk of acting at hazard, rather than putting that risk upon consumers who are, for the most part, totally helpless with respect to any violations. Speaking of this legislation in Smith v. California, this Court said, The public interest in the purity of its food is so great as to warrant the imposition of the highest standard of care on distributors, in fact, an absolute standard which will not hear a distributor's plea as to the amount of care he has used. These standards, which are embodied in the provisions of law we are discussing today, are vitally important since they deal with and govern the distribution of life-giving and life-saving drugs and medical devices, as well as foods. The Act thus imposes the highest duty of care known to the law, and it imposes upon those in a responsible position a duty to seek out possible violations to prevent them from occurring and correct them when they do occur. However, the reason for this is evident. Congress has judged that it is intolerable that there should be filth in our food or poison in our drugs or malfunction in our vital medical devices. It is for the failure to exercise this high duty of care and the failure to prevent the occurrence of violations that Congress imposes liability on corporate officers with a responsible relation to violations. Thus, in Dottowike, in the Dottowike case, the president of the Buffalo Pharmacal Company was held responsible for the shipment of understrength digitalis, even though the understrength characteristic of the digitalis occurred in the manufacture and not in the distribution, which was the business that Dottowike was in. It is for this reason that we believe that where there is a showing of a responsible relation to the violation and a showing of a violation, that the government has established a prima facie case. Now, that brings me to the matter of affirmative defenses. In the Wiesenfeld decision, this court suggested that an official might be in a position to raise a defense of powerlessness with respect to a violation. Now, I may have caused some confusion yesterday in discussing the term power. Of course, if power is viewed as authority merely, every chief executive officer has power. But power is something more than that. Power is the capacity to affect conditions in the world. And somebody with titular power, bending every effort to compliance, may nonetheless be unable to prevent some kind of violation. Now, this court has not articulated and not delineated the parameters of a possible defense of powerlessness. And it's our submission that this is not the case to do it in. Because however that defense may be conceived, on our view of the evidence, Park didn't raise it. Park's effort to establish that he reasonably relied on the advice of subordinates is refuted by the evidence in this case. Can you imagine or visualize any president and chief executive officer of a corporation being able to raise it? How can the chief executive officer of a corporation say, I'm sorry, I have no control over this corporation? He could not, of course, say, I have no control over the corporation. He could not, of course, say, I have no control over it in this respect. I mean, he just can't say that. In respect to a single instance or in respect to the willful conduct of a single individual, it's possible that the defense could be raised. Now, my feeling is that I don't know what the parameters of this defense might be. And if I were to engage in hypotheticals, it would be only that. Because this case presents an articulation of an attempt to defend on the ground that Park was entitled to rely upon his subordinates, subordinates, that he was entitled to rely upon his organizational structure and his system for dealing with sanitation problems. And the evidence in this case might be different if the case dealt with the first violation in the context of Mr. Justice Stewart's question. Well, I would say, first of all, and I hope to have time to get to this, that this case should be looked at in the context of the FDA criteria for prosecution. And they have in the act specifically appoints or requires the secretary to exercise discretion and not to prosecute for minor violations, or rather permits him not to prosecute for minor violations. And consistent with this, the FDA does not. And with respect to individuals, it is the FDA's policy only to prosecute individuals who, after they have received notice of a problem, have failed to take action that might correct it. So if we're speaking about a theory of criminal liability, I would say that a corporate executive without notice of a condition, if it was a condition which he could have corrected, would still be responsible. But the fact is, the FDA doesn't prosecute unless they have a good deal more. And as I say, this statute is unique in that it contemplates and specifically writes into the statute the exercise of prosecutorial discretion. So to get back to what you were speaking about a moment ago, I take it that the United States would not think that an executive would be shielded from liability under the statute, if he, even though he could demonstrate that he had a reasonably calculated system to affect acceptable results. I don't know. More specifically, I would gather you would not say it would be a defense if he proved that he gave a specific order. He knew about the situation and he gave a specific order to the warehouse superintendent to take these steps by a day after tomorrow. And the superintendent testifies in the case. He just completely refused to do it. He had something else to do and he just didn't want to do it that week. He just refused. I think that that would probably not be a defense, although I would say that that would be a jury question. He could say, he could attempt to persuade a jury that he was powerless in this regard. In our view... Well, everything's a jury question, a criminal case. Excuse me, Mr. Justice? Well, everything's a jury question in a criminal case. You can always argue to the jury, but that doesn't necessarily mean... Well, that's true. But this statute, I think, is, as the court viewed it in Dottorweick, really does envision the commitment of some of these issues to the judgment of the jury. As your honors are aware, the court refused in Dottorweick to articulate exactly what the parameters of the offense were, preferring to leave this matter to the judgment of prosecutors, to the guidance of trial judges, and the judgment of juries. Well, I think if you would think that the instruction that was given here was all right in this case and would be all right in any case. The instruction that was given here was not all right. In my view, Mr. Park woefully failed to do what he ought to have done in these circumstances. The instruction to the jury. Oh, I'm sorry. I was thinking of the instruction that Mr. Park did. No, no, no. The instruction to the jury. The instruction to the jury, I believe, was appropriate. And, in fact, if you compare it with the instruction in Dottorweick, which this court approved, I think you'll find that it follows the instruction in Dottorweick. I don't have time this morning to read line for line the two instructions, but they are in our brief, and the court can compare them. In fact, with that instruction, I take it the jury would be entitled to conclude that solely because a man is the chief executive officer of a company and has responsibility in the broadest sense, he can be held criminally liable for any kind of a failure to comply with the statute. If he has failed to make out an affirmative defense. Well, I still don't understand the affirmative defense unless it is to suggest that if a chief executive officer proves affirmatively, has the burden of going forward and proves to the jury that he's wholly incompetent and ineffective and should be fired from his job, there is no affirmative defense. Well, if he proved that he had a system which had always worked and through some malfunction in the system or the machinery, which he could not have dealt with and which no system could control, he would have perhaps shown that he was powerless with respect to that violation. I don't think all Park did here was to hand the matter to subordinates. He didn't discuss the matter with the vice president in charge of the Baltimore Division, and he took no steps to see that his instructions were complied with or the compliance was achieved. In consequence, we don't think whatever the defense might be, it was made out here. With the court's permission, I'd like to reserve the balance of my time for rebuttal. Mr. Harvey. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court, the respondent believes that the issue in this case is whether an individual may be convicted of a criminal offense without proof of any personal wrongdoing by that individual solely because of the individual's position as president of a corporation. I would not dwell on that point if it did not appear to me that overnight the government has somewhat retreated from its agreement with the questions asked by Mr. Justice Stewart and Mr. Justice White yesterday as to whether that was not in fact the government's position. I'm surprised that that retreat has occurred. I might refer you in the green amicus brief at page 17, the footnote at the bottom, what I believe to be an authentic quotation from Peter Barton Hutt, the assistant general counsel of HEW responsible for these matters, sitting at council table today, in which he says that the only exceptions he has in mind to that rule are the president's, quote, who spend their entire lives down in Florida and let some other guy run the company. I think that is the government's position. It was certainly the government's trial theory, and the difficulties which the Fourth Circuit saw in this case arise from that, having been the government's trial theory. I'll just make a few references to what does appear in the record. The indictment refers only—it was an information in five counts, not an indictment. The information refers only to Park as president. The government's response to Park's motion for a bill of particulars stated—it's in the appendix at 14 and 15— that the government's evidence, quote, would not show that the defendant personally performed the acts, close quotes, charged in the information, but, quote, will simply show that defendant was a corporate officer who, under law, bore a relationship to the receipt and storage of food, which would subject him to criminal liability, and then citing the Dottowicz decision. At some point, I take it you're going to tell us how the instruction here deviated from or fell short of the instruction approved in Dottowicz. Yes, certainly, and I'll go to that right now. I think that is important. The instruction approved in Dottowicz contained the critical language that the jury was to determine whether the acts had occurred under Dottowicz's supervision. That's the key sentence in the charge. I think that charge has to be placed in the context of the entire Dottowicz trial. Both sides have disagreed somewhat on that, but the record is, of course, available to you. Both sides have quoted from it. The issue tried in the Dottowicz case was not whether or not Mr. Dottowicz was responsible for what had occurred. He was the principal witness defending the position both of the corporation and of himself that no violations whatsoever had occurred. And as we've pointed out, and the Fourth Circuit found important, repeatedly in his testimony, Mr. Dottowicz and his counsel used the personal pronoun I or the personal pronoun you to refer to what the corporation had done in respect of the claimed violations. There was, throughout the testimony, almost an identity between the two. And I believe that that explains the jury verdict. The jury received evidence showing that Mr. Dottowicz, I, you, as he referred to himself, or as his counsel referred to him, had done these things and was mystified as to what, if anything, the corporation had done. Therefore, they convicted Dottowicz and not the corporation. In the context of that defense theory, in which the corporation denied all liability and Dottowicz was the principal spokesman for the corporation, the very short portion of the charge which deals with Dottowicz's personal liability was entirely appropriate. It was all that his counsel could possibly have asked for, and there was no objection to the charge. I think that charge is not an appropriate guideline for a case such as this case, in which the corporation pleaded guilty prior to trial, and there was no dispute that violations had occurred. Instead, the question was whether John Park was responsible for those violations. I think that was the problem which occurred. Mr. Harvey, what instruction did you offer on this point? The instruction which was offered by the defendant was, on this point, merely the instruction that his status as chief executive officer was not alone enough to convict him. It's quoted in the government brief. There's some history, however, which explains how that occurred. The trial judge throughout, at every critical stage of the proceeding, had indicated that he believed that under Dottowicz, the case must go to the jury, regardless almost of the evidence which had been presented. There was a colloquy in chambers concerning the charge. It is referred to in the record. But on the particular point, as to the appropriate instruction concerning responsibility, there was very vigorous exception taken to the charge. It appears in the record at Appendix 60. All the instruction you suggested was this bland rule about responsibility that you concretely presented to the court. There was nothing concretely presented to the court, Mr. Justice, because the court had indicated very strongly that he would not allow anything except what the... Does that relieve your responsibility of presenting it in making your record? No, it doesn't relieve... It does not relieve counsel of the necessity of taking exception to the charge as given. And that was very vigorously done. And the trial court at page 63 of the appendix cut off any further discussion of that exception, saying, quote, you have your objection, unquote, which I think in this context has some substantive importance. He did not wish to hear further about that point, because he believed that under Datterwijk he was required to give an instruction in the language taken from the opening sentences of Mr. Justice Murphy's dissent. And that was the theory of the prosecution in the trial court and the theory which the government had urged and which the trial court accepted. I want you to say, as the Fourth Circuit said, that the government not only tried it on the wrong theory, that is, that the president could be held criminally liable merely by reading the corporate bylaw and by presenting the Delaware corporate franchise tax returns to show that he was president, that that made out a case in chief, and that to take a charge from Mr. Justice Murphy's dissent in Datterwijk was not a proper charge in this case. I don't think that in this case the matter can be dealt with as one of harmless error in which you disregard several sentences of the charges of the charges of the charges of the charges. And then find on the basis of the entire record that Mr. Park had been found guilty. I think that you can find that the government was correct that the president is to be guilty solely because of his status as president. But that would imply approving the charge, and perhaps the charge did not go far enough. And I think, really, unless you accept the government's slight retreat, as I see it, either you should approve the charge and perhaps imply it could be strengthened, or you should follow the Fourth Circuit, require a new trial, and give guidance, which the trial courts appear to respond and to need after the passage of time since the Datterwijk decision, as to what the standard is. But I don't think the harmless error approach is appropriate, nor do I think the government urges that upon you either. I take it you think the Fourth Circuit properly characterized the infirmities of the charges given. Yes, I think the Fourth Circuit did. And I think the Fourth Circuit has laid down a very broad standard as to the type of evidence which would be appropriate to establish on a retrial that John Park was responsible for the violations charge, tying him, as the Fourth Circuit required, to the violations rather than tying him merely to the corporate hierarchy. I think it is a very broad standard. It will not be an easy case to win on retrial. I hardly think that the Fourth Circuit has made it difficult to convict presidents who are, in fact, responsible for the violations. But wasn't the trial judge tending to draw on Mr. Justice Frankfurter's majority opinion when he dealt with the concept of shared responsibility in the business process? Mr. Justice Frankfurter said whether an accused shares responsibility in the business process resulting in unlawful distribution and so forth. Part of the charge is taken from the opinion of this Court by Mr. Justice Frankfurter. The critical portions, in our view, and I refer to page 61 of the appendix, the critical portions are those opening sentences just below the middle of the page where the Court says, thirdly, that John R. Park held a position of authority in the operation of the business of acne markets, and then that sentence is repeated again in the next paragraph. That language comes directly from the dissent. Of course, if this Court believes that that fairly characterizes the dissent and you choose to reaffirm, daughter Weich, then that charge is good. It appears to us that it is bad, and in the government that portion of it is bad. And in the government's reply brief, the government seems to concede that that first sentence is not a satisfactory statement of the rule. That's at page 4 of the reply brief. Mr. Harvey, isn't it quite possible that a discussion may be perfectly appropriate for an appellate opinion and nonetheless not afford a suitable basis for charging the jury? I think that's exactly what happened here, and I urge that strongly on the Court of Appeals, that language was taken from a Frankfurter opinion, which was technical language, language intended for lawyers, it was, in the second part of the charge, used to instruct a jury, and I think it is very difficult to understand how a lay jury could have made any sense out of that second paragraph of the charge in this case, for that reason, just quoting from the opinion. What do you mean by the second paragraph? All right. By that, I mean the, I really mean the, what appears on page 62 of the appendix. It's the... The one that says that however the fact that... However the fact and so on... Yeah, as the chief executive does not require a fine... Right. And then it's the next sentences that are very, very difficult... Responsible relationship to the issue. Right. And that's language from the Frankfurter opinion. I think it's very difficult to... That does, perhaps, as difficult as you suggest, but that does go a little beyond merely the fact that he was chief executive officer, doesn't it? Oh, yes, it does. Even though he is, he still, you still have, the government still has to prove that he had a, something called a responsible relationship to the issue. That's correct. That is, that responsible relationship is nowhere defined. What you try, or trial counsel tried to have defined. That's what trial counsel was concerned about, and also concerned about the opening sentences. Now, if you compare this charge with the charge in cool, I think it's difficult to find that with these two opening sentences, this could be harmless error. But under this charge, I would suppose, if the jury concluded that this particular chief executive officer had responsibility for this area of the company's business, it could find him guilty for no reason other than the fact that he was the chief executive officer. I don't think it has to... The disclaimer is that the fact that the defendant is present and is a chief executive officer doesn't require the finding of guilt. Both sides tend to believe that what the judge actually said was president and chief executive officer, and that the transcript is not correct on that point. But if you go back to the opening sentences, there is nothing in those sentences to the effect that the authority and responsibility has to be in relation to the offenses. That's the language on page 61. And it's that language on page 61 which the Court of Appeals found most prejudicial. Well, do you say that the language at the top of page 62 of the appendix... Yes, Your Honor. ...the language had a responsible relation to the situation, even though he may not have participated personally. Do you say that that goes beyond Datterwick or that it is... No, I say that does not go beyond Datterwick. I think that is very bad language in which to instruct a jury so that the jury understands what the issue is. I think it's the error of taking language from an appellate opinion and using it directly as a jury instruction, which I was discussing with Mr. Justice Friend. If the court had a responsible relation, does that not mean clearly had a relationship of responsibility? Any difficulty reading that? Well, it can be understood that way. Can be? Yes. What other way could it be understood? I should make clear that I would not, had this portion of the charge been given without the language which appears on page 61, it is, in my opinion, certain that the Fourth Circuit would not have reversed. It's the language on page 61 that is the language which seemed to be critical. Which language? Yes. The language is, thirdly, that John R. Park held a position of authority in the operation of the business of Acme Markets, Incorporated, and then repeated again in the next paragraph, given as a summary of the elements which the jury must find. I think it's as a summary that is an important factor. That language comes directly from the government's third request for charge, which appears in the appendix at page 72, and it is also quoted directly from Mr. Justice Murphy's dissent. Do you question that Mr. Park held a position of authority in the operation of the business of Acme Markets? I do not question that he did. He was selected to be prosecuted because he was chief executive officer. Therefore, we contend that this sentence amounts to a directed verdict of guilty. Select the man who's chief executive officer. Tell the jury that if he has a position of authority and responsibility, he may be convicted. He is convicted. That's what we object to. Wasn't he also made aware of what was going on? Well, the government has... The government made him aware, but the only count which charges conduct occurring after the letter to Mr. Park is conduct which the government factually cannot prove occurred after that letter. In other words, the fifth count... Did you put on evidence that he wasn't made aware? No, I didn't. We didn't put on... He was in your possession, wasn't he? Park was in your possession. He was made aware officially by the government of the conditions. There is four counts occurred before that notice. The fifth count was discovered in an inspection which occurred after the notice, but the government cannot prove that the violation occurred after the notice. It was discovered after the notice, but the time frame in which the rodents gnawed that particular package may have occurred three weeks before the notice. That's why the government makes no distinction. Did the government mark your own testimony as to what he did to correct the situation? Yes, he did. And the testimony is in the appendix that he delegated to the appropriate persons the resolution of the problem. He wanted only to if he had the responsibility to do it. Right? Well, the responsibility... He acknowledged a general responsibility. He had also received specific notice from the government, and I think he reacted reasonably to that notice. But that, I think, does not go to the question of the charge, which is the only matter on which the Fourth Circuit reversed. We argued there was not sufficient evidence. We never reached that point and did order a new trial. I'd like to turn briefly to the constitutional limitations which this case may present, depending upon whether the court desires to, as a respondent believes, who, as a respondent believes, go substantially beyond Dottweich. And I would urge first that this court's determination of whether a prosecution under the act is subject to ordinary criminal constitutional limitations should not depend either on the absence of a sentence of imprisonment or on the relatively light fine which was imposed by the trial judge. It would be ironic if the light fine was used to justify the conviction because the light fine reflects the trial court's view of the weight of the government's case, as the trial court commented. It was $50 a count against a maximum of $1,000 a count. I think, second, the court should consider that the government desires to have all the benefits of a criminal conviction. The government, in its reply brief, at pages 9 and 10, urges that it must have criminal sanctions to enforce this act. I think this court should therefore hold the government to that. If the government wants the stigma of a criminal conviction, wants the threat of a substantial sentence of imprisonment, wants the threat of a felony record on a second conviction, the government should be required to adhere to the same criminal standards which govern every other prosecution. Nor is there any logical reason why a special rule should be elaborated merely for Food and Drug Act cases. Certainly the government, when other statutes are at issue, does not take the position that Dottweich applies only to Food and Drug Act cases. It's been applied and freed to firearms registration. The O'Keefe article, which both sides have cited, includes an appendix listing dozens of other statutes which might receive a similar interpretation. It's not properly a special problem for Food and Drug Act cases. If respondent is correct that it is a criminal case, then under Winship, the accused is protected against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged. It appears to respondent that the concept which the government advanced at trial, advanced in the Fourth Circuit, and advanced here, that somehow there is a standard of proof which gets to the jury and there is a different standard of proof which might be the standard for conviction, which I think is the substance of their argument, is not one which is justifiable in a criminal case. Nor can the sentence in Weisenfeld be relied upon to create a doctrine of affirmative defenses applicable to individuals, most especially because the Weisenfeld case involved only a corporation, as my brother forgot in his prior argument. Although the case speaks of a public warehouse man, it is a corporation which is involved. And furthermore, the powerlessness issue which was discussed there had no application to individuals charged with offenses, went merely to defenses which might be available to a corporation. We would say, lastly, that going back to scales and other cases, this court has never favored and has gone to some lengths to disfavor punishment imposed merely upon a status. In this case, the government sought to do that. The Fourth Circuit has laid down a rule which requires instead, and in our view consistently with Dottweich, that the acts of the individual, either by omission or commission, which directly or constructively cause the offense, be the evidence necessary to convict. Well, under that theory, only the rats would be liable, wouldn't it? No, I think under that theory, many chief executive officers in this situation, and perhaps respondent John Park, might be found guilty. I think that is a standard which gives the government very ample room to convict when there has, in fact, been a violation of the act. And the government's own standards, as have been pointed out in the briefs, show that the government has rarely, if ever, until this case, commenced a prosecution in which they did not attempt to present exactly that evidence tying the individual directly to the violations. How could they do that unless they put 24-hour surveillance on him from the time he first got notice of the event and up to the time that they charged him? You don't expect that the government can know what he's doing except as he writes memos and gives orders which are documented by tangible evidence. Well, his omissions to act under the Fourth Circuit decision are equally proof of his personal liability for what has occurred within his corporation. I think that's a key part of the decision which has been overlooked in the government's brief. You would say that if it were proved he knew of it and had an opportunity to cure the defect and didn't, that that's a far different situation than this instruction would permit. Absolutely. And I do not mean by responding that way to your question to imply that your question limits the other evidence which the government might show because notice or knowledge is not a necessary part of the government's case either. I think the government has misunderstood the opinion on that point and as we pointed out also appears to have misunderstood the Abbott opinion which is referred to in both degrees. Are you making any kind of a constitutional argument here? Let's just assume the statute said in plain language any chief executive officer if under the bylaws has general responsibility for the situation that has been found to be defective or vulnerable under the statute. Yes, I am making a due process argument there. I think that as to an individual that a statute which wrote into the text of the statute what the government attempted to do here in this trial that has proved merely the bylaw and proved that he was president that that statute would not be constitutional. I don't think Dottweitz did that. We've urged the reasons why not and therefore we support the Fourth Circuit's reversal. Very well, Mr. Harvey. Before you commence what effect if any do you give in your analysis of this problem the statute and how it should be applied to the size and complexity of the corporation? This corporation involved 35,000 employees and 900 stores scattered all over the United States. it seems to me to be one thing to hold a corporate executive responsible if he has a very small organization and sits right on top of it and either knows or ought to know what goes on from day to day but if you have a corporation of this size and the others much larger would this statute apply? The size and increasing complexity of the business of handling these kinds of sensitive commodities is an argument for applying the statute in the strictest sense to the highest corporate official who has responsibility it's the only way that we are going to have a total commitment by the corporation to compliance with the act if we can use size as a shield from responsibility then the FDA simply will not be able to induce companies to comply with the act by holding highest corporate officials responsible we do create a strong incentive in that end excuse me does this record show how many warehouses they have? yes they had 12 warehouses and 4 special warehouses according to the record and some 800 were all relating to warehouses were they? these violations yes they were relating to inspections of warehouses if I may with only the few minutes I have I would like to address myself initially to the question of the Park case itself it seems to us that if respondent Park is not guilty under this statute no one is I think we have failed to pay adequate attention to the evidence in this case Park received notice in 1970 fully a year more than a year before the violation in Baltimore of the fact that his system for handling sanitation matters had abysmably failed in Philadelphia and he nonetheless relied upon the same subordinates in the same system and allowed the same
